body:
The Harappan civilisation extended into Gujarat

The Harappan civilisation, also called the Indus civilisation, was one of the earliest urban civilisations of the Indian subcontinent. Its Mature Harappan phase is generally dated to approximately 2600–1900 BCE. Harappan settlements extended beyond the Indus River valley into several regions, including present-day Gujarat.

Gujarat formed an important part of this settlement network. Its coastal areas provided access to the Arabian Sea, while its inland regions supplied agricultural products, stones, minerals and other materials. Harappan communities established settlements at different locations according to the resources and geographical advantages available there.

The settlements were not all identical. Some were associated with specialised crafts and exchange, some had substantial defensive walls, and others preserve evidence of regional Harappan traditions. This explains why identifying a Harappan site requires more than remembering that it belongs to the Indus civilisation: its location and distinctive finds must also be understood.

Five important sites and their locations

SiteLocation in GujaratPrincipal association
LothalAhmedabad district, near the Gulf of KhambhatLarge basin conventionally identified as a dockyard; bead workshop, warehouse, seals and sealings
SurkotadaKutch district, near RaparFortified citadel and residential area; disputed identification of horse remains
Desalpar (Gunthli)Nakhatrana area, Kutch districtMassive stone fortification; inscribed seals and a terracotta sealing
RangpurLimbdi area, Surendranagar districtHarappan and later pottery traditions; evidence of regional cultural continuity
RojdiGondal area, Rajkot districtRegional Harappan settlement; characteristic pottery, beads and copper objects

Three geographical groups to remember

Lothal and the Gulf of Khambhat

Lothal lies in the Ahmedabad region, close to the Gulf of Khambhat. Its position near an ancient watercourse helps explain its association with movement of goods. It is especially important for the study of Harappan craft production and maritime exchange.

Surkotada and Desalpar in Kutch

Surkotada and Desalpar are both situated in Kutch. Each has evidence of fortification, but their distinguishing discoveries are different. Surkotada is associated with a fortified settlement and controversial animal-bone identifications. Desalpar is particularly notable for its substantial stone defensive wall and inscribed objects.

Rangpur and Rojdi in Saurashtra

Rangpur and Rojdi lie in the broader Saurashtra region. Rangpur is in present-day Surendranagar district, whereas Rojdi is in Rajkot district. Both provide evidence of Harappan traditions in regional settlements, including pottery that helps distinguish different stages of occupation.

Why location and function must be distinguished

The Harappans used land routes, rivers and coastal waters for communication and exchange. A site connected with this wider network was not necessarily a seaport. For example, finding beads or seals at a settlement demonstrates participation in Harappan material culture, but it does not by itself establish that ships entered that settlement.

Similarly, the presence of a defensive wall indicates that a settlement was fortified; it does not establish that the settlement was a maritime trading centre. Such distinctions are essential when matching sites with their discoveries.

Prelims focus

  • Mature Harappan civilisation: approximately 2600–1900 BCE.
  • Lothal: Ahmedabad district; large basin, bead-making and trade-related remains.
  • Surkotada and Desalpar: both in Kutch.
  • Rangpur: Surendranagar district, near Limbdi.
  • Rojdi: Rajkot district, near Gondal.
  • Trap: Not every Harappan settlement in Gujarat was a port.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones', pp. 1–2, 10–12; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, ch. 2, site map preceding p. 9; Gujarat Tourism, 'Lothal' and 'Surkotada Indus Valley Civilization', consulted 17 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, Indian Archaeology 1963–64—A Review, pp. 10–12, published 1967; Archaeological Survey of India, Indian Archaeology 1993–94—A Review, p. 40, published 2000; S. R. Rao, 'Excavation at Rangpur and Other Explorations in Gujarat', Ancient India, nos. 18–19, 1963, pp. 5–13.]

title: Harappan Sites in Gujarat: Historical Background and Geographical Distribution

body:
Lothal's geographical setting

Lothal is a Harappan settlement in present-day Ahmedabad district of Gujarat, approximately 80 km southwest of Ahmedabad. It was situated near an ancient watercourse associated with the Sabarmati river system and the Gulf of Khambhat.

The settlement's location matters because Harappan communities transported goods over land, along rivers and through coastal waters. Access to waterways could connect a town with other settlements and more distant trading regions. Lothal's craft workshops and storage-related structures make this geographical setting particularly significant.

The large rectangular basin

One of Lothal's most prominent remains is a large, brick-lined, rectangular basin on the eastern side of the settlement. The Class 6 textbook Exploring Society: India and Beyond describes it as approximately 217 m long and 36 m wide. Published descriptions give somewhat different measurements, so these figures should be understood as approximate.

The basin is a physical archaeological structure. Its existence is not disputed. The important question concerns its original function.

Why it is conventionally called a dockyard

A dockyard, in the context of ancient trade, is a facility where boats could enter or be received for activities such as loading and unloading goods. The conventional interpretation of Lothal's basin is that it functioned as a tidal dock or harbour basin.

Under this interpretation, boats could have approached through a water channel connected with the Gulf of Khambhat. Water entering at suitable tidal conditions may have helped vessels reach the basin. Goods could then have been transferred between boats, storage areas and the settlement.

The basin's size, adjoining structures and ancient waterway setting help explain why the dockyard interpretation became widely accepted in textbooks and official descriptions.

Why the basin's function is debated

Although the basin is conventionally identified as a dockyard, its use as a harbour is not established beyond dispute. Some researchers have proposed that it served as a reservoir or another form of water-storage structure.

The difference is important. A dockyard receives vessels and supports transport activities, whereas a reservoir primarily stores water. Both may be large, carefully constructed basins. Their appearance alone does not settle which function was intended.

A 2024 study of the ancient landscape around Lothal identified a connection with a former course of the Sabarmati River. This strengthens the geographical case for water access to the settlement. However, identifying a former river connection is not the same as proving exactly how the basin was used.

What is established and what is interpreted?

  • Established: Lothal has a large rectangular basin and other substantial Harappan remains.
  • Supported geographical connection: The site was associated with an ancient watercourse near the Gulf of Khambhat.
  • Conventional interpretation: The basin served as a dockyard or harbour facility.
  • Alternative interpretation: The basin may have been used for water storage.

Lothal in the wider maritime network

The Harappans had contacts with regions around the Arabian Sea. Lothal's location and commercial remains are consistent with a role in exchange through Gujarat's coastal network. They help explain why it is commonly described as a Harappan port town.

However, the dockyard interpretation should not be turned into a stronger claim than the evidence supports. It would be inaccurate to state that every vessel travelling between the Harappan world and West Asia necessarily passed through Lothal.

Prelims focus

  • Lothal: a Harappan settlement in Ahmedabad district, Gujarat.
  • Geographical association: ancient Sabarmati watercourse and Gulf of Khambhat.
  • Major structure: a large rectangular brick-lined basin.
  • Textbook dimensions: approximately 217 m by 36 m.
  • Conventional identification: dockyard or tidal harbour basin.
  • Trap: The existence of the basin is certain; its precise function remains debated.

[NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, ch. 4, 'In the Earliest Cities', p. 39, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, ch. 6, 'The Beginnings of Indian Civilisation', pp. 97–99; Gujarat Tourism, 'Lothal', consulted 17 November 2026; Shereen Ratnagar, 'Lothal in the History of the Indian Ocean', Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Asian History, 17 April 2024; Ekta Gupta, V. N. Prabhakar and Vikrant Jain, 'Sabarmati and its connection with the Harappan port Lothal and the Nal corridor', Journal of Archaeological Science, vol. 170, article 106046, October 2024.]

title: Lothal's Large Basin: The Dockyard Interpretation and Its Limits

body:
Lothal was an important centre of craft production

Lothal is associated with the production of objects made from stone, shell and metal. Its location was advantageous because materials used in these crafts were available within Gujarat or could be obtained through regional exchange.

One important material was carnelian, a reddish semi-precious stone used for making beads and ornaments. The Bharuch region of Gujarat was among the sources of carnelian available to Harappan craftspeople. Other materials, including steatite and metals, could be obtained from different regions.

The bead-making workshop

Excavations at Lothal revealed a building interpreted as a bead-making workshop. Finds included pieces of stone, unfinished beads, tools associated with bead production and completed beads.

These discoveries are important because they indicate more than possession of ornaments. Finished beads alone might have been brought from elsewhere. The occurrence of unfinished objects together with tools and raw material supports the conclusion that beads were manufactured at Lothal.

Harappan craftspeople shaped, polished and drilled beads so that they could be strung together. Some of these finished objects could be used locally, while others could be carried to different settlements.

The warehouse and the movement of goods

Lothal also had a structure conventionally identified as a warehouse or storehouse. Its importance is strengthened by the discovery of numerous seals and sealings in the associated remains.

A warehouse is a building used for keeping goods before they are distributed, consumed or transported. In a settlement involved in exchange, storage would help organise goods arriving from different places or awaiting further movement.

The presence of a warehouse-like structure does not establish the precise contents of every package kept there. Nevertheless, it fits the broader evidence that Lothal was a craft-producing and trade-connected settlement.

Seals and sealings: two different objects

A seal is an object carrying an engraved design or signs that can be pressed into a soft material to leave an impression. Harappan seals were commonly made of steatite, a soft stone, and often carried animal motifs together with signs of the Harappan script.

A sealing is the impression left by a seal on clay or another suitable material. The two terms must not be treated as interchangeable.

How a sealing could secure goods

  1. A bag or package containing goods was closed and tied.
  2. Wet clay was applied over the knot or fastening.
  3. A seal was pressed into the clay, leaving an impression.
  4. If the clay sealing reached its destination intact, it suggested that the fastening had not been opened during transport.

The impression could also help identify the person or group associated with the goods. Because the Harappan script remains undeciphered, the exact meaning of the signs on individual seals cannot be stated with certainty.

Seal and sealing are not synonyms

Seal: the engraved object used to make an impression.

Sealing: the impression left in clay or another soft material.

Lothal and long-distance trade

Harappan exchange networks connected settlements within the subcontinent and extended towards regions around the Arabian Sea. Archaeological finds and Mesopotamian texts indicate contacts involving areas associated with present-day Oman, Bahrain and Mesopotamia.

Mesopotamian records refer to a region called Meluhha, commonly regarded as possibly referring to the Harappan region. They mention goods such as carnelian and other valuable materials. The evidence is consistent with maritime exchange, although the exact identification of Meluhha and the routes taken by individual shipments require caution.

Lothal's bead-making industry, seals, sealings and storage-related remains show how a Gujarat settlement could participate in a wider system of production and exchange. They do not prove that every Harappan object found in West Asia originated specifically from Lothal.

The relationship between production and trade

Lothal demonstrates the connection between several activities. Craftspeople obtained raw materials and produced finished goods. Traders could collect and transport these goods. Storage areas could hold materials awaiting movement, while seals and sealings could help identify and secure packages.

These activities explain why beads, the warehouse, seals and the possible dockyard are studied together. They represent different parts of a trade-connected settlement, not four names for the same feature.

Prelims focus

  • Lothal: associated with bead-making, shell and metal crafts.
  • Carnelian: reddish semi-precious stone used for beads; the Bharuch region was an important source.
  • Workshop evidence: raw pieces, unfinished beads, tools and completed beads.
  • Warehouse: structure associated with numerous seals and sealings.
  • Harappan script: remains undeciphered.
  • Trap: A seal is the engraved object; a sealing is its impression.

[NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, ch. 4, 'In the Earliest Cities', pp. 39–40, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones', pp. 10–16; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, ch. 2, 'Arts of the Indus Valley', pp. 11–15; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, ch. 6, pp. 97–99; Archaeological Survey of India, Lothal: A Harappan Port Town, 1955–62, vol. 1, section on the warehouse; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Archaeological remains of a Harappa Port-Town, Lothal', Tentative List entry 5918, consulted 17 November 2026.]
